stem:
A 27-year-old woman has her third outbreak of genital herpes this year, confirmed by swab when it first occurred. She has been in a faithful relationship for two years and asks whether her partner must be giving it back to her each time.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Her partner is reinfecting her at each outbreak
options.B: The virus was fully cleared after the first episode and these are new infections
options.C: The recurrences are due to a secondary bacterial infection of the skin
options.D: The virus lies dormant in sensory nerve ganglia and periodically reactivates
options.E: Small amounts of virus persist permanently on the surface of the skin

correct_answer: D. The virus lies dormant in sensory nerve ganglia and periodically reactivates
why_correct: After primary infection, herpes simplex virus travels along sensory nerves and establishes lifelong latency in the dorsal root (sacral) ganglia. Triggers such as stress, illness or menstruation can cause reactivation, with virus travelling back down the nerve to the skin. Recurrences therefore come from her own latent virus rather than a new infection, and frequent episodes can be managed with suppressive aciclovir. Source: UK national guideline for the management of anogenital herpes, BASHH, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Reinfection is not needed to explain recurrences, which come from her own latent virus. B. HSV is never cleared after the primary episode. C. Recurrences are viral, not bacterial. E. Between episodes the virus resides in nerve ganglia; asymptomatic shedding occurs intermittently but the reservoir is neural, not the skin surface.
pearl: Recurrent episodes are usually milder and shorter than the first, and often preceded by a prodrome of tingling or burning.
thinking: Recurrent confirmed genital herpes ↓ Worry about reinfection by her partner ↓ HSV establishes latency after primary infection ↓ Reservoir is the sensory ganglia ↓ Reactivation causes recurrences
exam_trap: A, Reinfection by her partner — it seems a logical explanation for repeated episodes, but recurrences come from reactivation of her own latent virus.
takeaway: Herpes simplex remains latent in sensory ganglia for life and recurrences reflect reactivation, not reinfection.

stem:
A theatre nurse attends the occupational health department two days after blood from an HIV-positive patient splashed into her eye during an emergency laparotomy. She rinsed her eye at the time but did not report the incident until today. The source patient had recently stopped antiretroviral therapy and his viral load is detectable.

What should be offered now?

options.A: Reassurance only, because conjunctival exposure carries no meaningful HIV risk
options.B: Baseline HIV test with a repeat in three months and no further treatment
options.C: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin as the priority intervention
options.D: A 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis started as soon as possible today
options.E: No intervention, because the window for any preventive treatment has already passed

correct_answer: D. A 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis started as soon as possible today
why_correct: Mucous membrane exposure to blood from a source with a detectable HIV viral load is a recognised indication for post-exposure prophylaxis. PEP should start as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, but it can still be considered up to 72 hours after the exposure. At two days she is within that window, so a 28-day course should be started today alongside baseline testing and follow-up. Source: UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, BASHH/BHIVA, 2021 (2023 amendment).
why_wrong: A. Conjunctival splashes do carry a small transmission risk and are an accepted indication for PEP when the source is viraemic. B. Testing alone wastes the chance to prevent infection while she is still within the treatment window. C. Hepatitis B immunoglobulin addresses hepatitis B, not HIV, and the source is known to have HIV. E. PEP can still be started up to 72 hours after exposure, so the window has not closed.
pearl: PEP is not usually recommended when the source patient is on antiretroviral therapy with a confirmed undetectable viral load, because the risk of transmission is negligible.
thinking: Blood splash to a mucous membrane ↓ Source HIV-positive with detectable viral load ↓ Significant exposure, so PEP is indicated ↓ Presenting at 48 hours is still within the 72-hour window ↓ Start a 28-day course today with baseline testing
exam_trap: E, No intervention because the window has passed — the delay in reporting makes it feel too late, but PEP can still be started up to 72 hours after exposure.
takeaway: After a significant HIV exposure, start PEP as soon as possible, and it remains worthwhile up to 72 hours afterwards.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman has a reactive fourth-generation HIV test confirmed at the sexual health clinic. Before discussing treatment and the need for prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, the team wants to know how far her immune system has been damaged.

Which blood test gives this information?
why_correct: HIV destroys CD4 helper T lymphocytes, so the absolute CD4 count is the standard measure of how immunocompromised a person is. It guides the risk of opportunistic infections and decisions such as starting co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and it is monitored alongside viral load once treatment starts. Source: Guidelines for the routine investigation and monitoring of adults living with HIV, BHIVA, 2019.
why_wrong: B. The total white cell count is too non-specific and can be normal despite a very low CD4 count. C. Immunoglobulins are often raised in HIV and do not reflect cellular immune damage. D. CRP reflects inflammation, not immune competence. E. p24 antigen is useful for early diagnosis but does not measure immune suppression.
pearl: The CD4 count shows immune damage, whereas the HIV viral load shows how well antiretroviral therapy is suppressing the virus.
thinking: Confirmed HIV infection ↓ Question is about degree of immune damage ↓ HIV targets CD4 helper T cells ↓ CD4 count reflects immunosuppression ↓ Viral load is used for treatment response
exam_trap: E, HIV p24 antigen level — it is an HIV-specific test so it seems relevant, but it helps with early diagnosis and does not measure immune damage.
takeaway: The CD4 count is the measure of immune suppression in HIV.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy who has not received any MMR vaccines is brought to the emergency department. A week ago he developed painful swelling of both parotid glands, and over the last day he has had a worsening headache, has vomited several times and finds bright light uncomfortable. He is alert, his neck is stiff on flexion and there is no rash.

Which complication is most likely?

options.A: Bacterial parotitis spreading to the deep neck

why_correct: Mumps virus commonly invades the central nervous system, and aseptic meningitis is one of its most frequent complications, usually appearing within about a week of the parotitis, although it can occur before or without parotid swelling. Headache, vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness in an alert, unvaccinated teenager with recent bilateral parotid swelling fit this well. The illness is usually self-limiting, but bacterial meningitis must still be considered and excluded. Source: Mumps, Green Book chapter 23, UKHSA, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Deep neck infection would cause neck swelling, trismus and systemic toxicity rather than meningism. B. Pancreatitis causes upper abdominal pain and vomiting but not photophobia or neck stiffness. C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage has a sudden thunderclap onset and is not linked to mumps. D. Orchitis causes a painful swollen testis, not headache and meningism.
pearl: Mumps is a notifiable disease in the UK, and outbreaks still occur in teenagers and young adults who missed one or both MMR doses.
thinking: Unvaccinated teenager ↓ Bilateral parotitis a week ago ↓ Now headache, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness ↓ Alert with no rash ↓ Mumps aseptic meningitis
exam_trap: D, Mumps orchitis — it is the best-known complication of mumps in males, but it causes testicular pain and swelling, not meningism.
takeaway: Meningism a few days after mumps parotitis suggests aseptic viral meningitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: softened timing of mumps meningitis (within about a week of parotitis; can precede or occur without it)

presentation: Blood cultures in suspected bacterial meningitis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a high fever, intense headache and neck stiffness that came on over the last 12 hours. Bacterial meningitis is suspected. She is conscious, her airway is safe and she has no rash.

Which investigation should be taken without delay as part of her first assessment?

options.B: Throat swab for viral PCR only

why_correct: In suspected bacterial meningitis, blood cultures should be taken promptly, before the first dose of antibiotics, because they often identify the organism even when a lumbar puncture is delayed or done after treatment has started. Taking them must not hold up intravenous antibiotics, which should be given within an hour of arrival. Whole-blood meningococcal and pneumococcal PCR, CRP and glucose are sent at the same time, and a lumbar puncture is done when it is safe. Source: Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease, NICE NG240, 2024.
why_wrong: A. MRI is not part of the initial assessment and would delay care. B. A throat swab is sent for meningococcal culture, not for viral PCR alone, and it does not replace blood cultures. C. An EEG is not needed unless seizure activity is suspected. E. ESR is non-specific and does not influence immediate management.
pearl: If antibiotics have already been given before a lumbar puncture, blood and CSF PCR for meningococcus and pneumococcus can still confirm the cause.
thinking: Fever, headache and neck stiffness ↓ Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Need to identify the organism ↓ Take blood cultures promptly ↓ Do not delay antibiotics while sampling
exam_trap: A, MRI scan of the brain — brain imaging feels thorough for a neurological illness, but it is not a first-line test and would delay treatment.
takeaway: Take blood cultures promptly in suspected bacterial meningitis, without delaying antibiotics.

stem:
A 26-year-old man is reviewed on the acute medical unit with two days of headache, dislike of bright light and pain on bending his neck forward. He is orientated, his blood pressure and heart rate are normal, and there are no focal signs. A lumbar puncture is performed. The CSF is clear, with a raised white cell count made up mainly of lymphocytes, a normal glucose ratio and a mildly raised protein.

Which diagnosis best fits these findings?
why_correct: Clear CSF with a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and only a slightly raised protein is the typical pattern of viral meningitis. Combined with a well, orientated young man with stable observations, this is the best fit. Enteroviruses are the most frequent cause in the UK. Source: UK joint specialist societies guideline on the diagnosis and management of acute meningitis in adults, British Infection Association, 2016.
why_wrong: B. Bacterial meningitis usually gives turbid CSF with neutrophils, low glucose and high protein. C. Tuberculous meningitis has lymphocytes but a markedly low glucose and very high protein, often with a subacute course. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a thunderclap headache and blood or xanthochromia in the CSF. E. Migraine does not produce a CSF pleocytosis.
pearl: Partially treated bacterial meningitis can shift the CSF towards lymphocytes, so a history of recent antibiotics makes the CSF harder to interpret.
thinking: Meningism in a well young adult ↓ Clear CSF ↓ Lymphocytes predominate ↓ Normal glucose, slightly raised protein ↓ Viral meningitis
exam_trap: C, Tuberculous meningitis — it also gives a lymphocytic CSF, but the glucose would be low and the protein very high, which is not the case here.
takeaway: Lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose points to viral meningitis.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman who stopped her antiretroviral therapy two years ago is brought in by her sister. For the past three weeks she has had a slowly worsening headache, low-grade fevers and, more recently, episodes of confusion. Her last CD4 count was very low. There is minimal neck stiffness and no focal weakness.

Which opportunistic infection should be considered first?
why_correct: Cryptococcus neoformans causes a subacute meningitis in people with advanced HIV, typically with a headache that builds over weeks, fever and altered mental state, often with little meningism. Raised intracranial pressure is common. The diagnosis is made with serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, and the opening pressure should be measured at lumbar puncture. Source: Guidelines for the treatment of opportunistic infection in HIV-seropositive individuals, BHIVA/BIA, 2011.
why_wrong: A. Pneumocystis pneumonia presents with exertional breathlessness, dry cough and hypoxia rather than headache and confusion. B. CMV retinitis causes floaters and visual loss. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes painful swallowing. E. Disseminated MAC causes fever, weight loss, diarrhoea and anaemia rather than a meningitic picture.
pearl: Raised CSF opening pressure is common in cryptococcal meningitis and repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures may be needed to relieve it.
thinking: Untreated HIV with a very low CD4 count ↓ Headache building over weeks ↓ Fever and confusion with little meningism ↓ Subacute fungal meningitis ↓ Cryptococcal meningitis
exam_trap: E, Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex — it also occurs at very low CD4 counts with fever, but it does not usually cause headache and confusion.
takeaway: A subacute headache with fever and confusion in advanced HIV suggests cryptococcal meningitis.

stem:
In late summer, a 22-year-old woman attends the GP surgery with a three-day history of fever, a frontal headache and discomfort looking at light. Her younger brother had a similar illness last week. She is alert, has no rash and no focal signs, and is later confirmed to have viral meningitis.

Which group of viruses is the most common cause in the UK?
why_correct: Enteroviruses, such as echoviruses and coxsackieviruses, are the most frequent cause of viral meningitis in the UK. They are spread by the faecal-oral and respiratory routes, cluster in families and peak in summer and autumn. Most cases resolve with supportive care. Source: UK joint specialist societies guideline on the diagnosis and management of acute meningitis in adults, British Infection Association, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Herpes simplex type 1 is the classic cause of encephalitis rather than common viral meningitis; type 2 more often causes meningitis. B. Epstein-Barr virus rarely causes meningitis. D. Influenza is not a common cause of meningitis. E. Rabies causes a fatal encephalitis, not meningitis, and classical rabies is not acquired in the UK.
pearl: Viral meningitis caused by herpes simplex type 2 can recur, a pattern sometimes called Mollaret meningitis.
thinking: Fever, headache, photophobia in an alert young adult ↓ Confirmed viral meningitis ↓ Late summer timing and a sick sibling ↓ Common seasonal, family-clustering viruses ↓ Enteroviruses
exam_trap: A, Herpes simplex virus type 1 — herpes viruses are linked with CNS infection, but HSV-1 is the typical cause of encephalitis, not of common viral meningitis.
takeaway: Enteroviruses are the most common cause of viral meningitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong E: rabies causes encephalitis not meningitis; 'classical rabies' not acquired in UK (bat lyssavirus exists)

stem:
The practice nurse is planning a recall campaign for the routine shingles (herpes zoster) vaccine at a GP surgery. She checks which patients the NHS routine programme is aimed at.

Which group is it mainly designed to protect?

options.C: Healthcare workers with no history of chickenpox
options.D: Pregnant women in the third trimester

correct_answer: E. Older adults at specified ages
why_correct: Reactivation of varicella zoster virus becomes more frequent with age as cell-mediated immunity declines, and older people have the highest rates of shingles and post-herpetic neuralgia. In England the routine programme offers two doses of the non-live recombinant vaccine to adults when they turn 65 or 70, with catch-up until their 80th birthday, and to severely immunosuppressed adults from age 18. Source: Shingles vaccination eligibility, UKHSA, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Infants are not offered shingles vaccine; their routine schedule covers other infections. B. Adolescents are offered vaccines such as HPV and MenACWY, not shingles vaccine. C. Non-immune healthcare workers are offered varicella (chickenpox) vaccine, which is different. D. Pregnant women are offered pertussis and RSV vaccines, not shingles vaccine.
pearl: The non-live recombinant shingles vaccine (Shingrix) can be given to immunosuppressed people, who cannot receive live vaccines.
thinking: Shingles is reactivation of varicella zoster virus ↓ Cell-mediated immunity wanes with age ↓ Incidence and post-herpetic neuralgia rise in older people ↓ Programme targets older adults ↓ Immunosuppressed people also eligible
exam_trap: C, Healthcare workers with no history of chickenpox — they are offered a varicella-related vaccine, but it is chickenpox vaccine, not shingles vaccine.
takeaway: The UK shingles programme targets older adults because shingles risk rises with age.

presentation: Anaphylaxis to a previous vaccine dose
stem:
The mother of a 4-month-old girl brings her for the next dose of a routine vaccine. The records show that minutes after the previous dose of the same vaccine the baby developed widespread hives, wheeze and floppiness, and was treated with intramuscular adrenaline in the surgery.

What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Give the dose today and observe her in the waiting room for 15 minutes
options.B: Give it after a dose of oral chlorphenamine
options.C: Withhold further doses until specialist advice is obtained
options.D: Split the dose into two halves given 30 minutes apart
options.E: Give the dose with a short course of oral prednisolone

correct_answer: C. Withhold further doses until specialist advice is obtained
why_correct: A confirmed anaphylactic reaction to a previous dose of a vaccine, or to one of its components, means further doses of that vaccine should be avoided unless a specialist advises otherwise. Hives, wheeze and collapse treated with adrenaline is anaphylaxis. The vaccine should be withheld and specialist advice sought, for example from an immunologist or paediatric allergy service, about alternatives or supervised vaccination. Source: Contraindications and special considerations, Green Book chapter 6, UKHSA, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Routine observation does not make it safe to repeat a vaccine that caused anaphylaxis. B. Antihistamine premedication does not prevent anaphylaxis and may mask early signs. D. Splitting the dose is not an accepted approach and still exposes her to the trigger. E. Steroid cover does not prevent anaphylaxis.
pearl: Minor local reactions, mild fever, family history of allergy and egg allergy are generally not contraindications to routine vaccines.
thinking: Previous dose caused hives, wheeze and collapse ↓ Treated with adrenaline, so anaphylaxis ↓ Anaphylaxis to the same vaccine is a contraindication ↓ Withhold the dose ↓ Seek specialist advice
exam_trap: B, Give it after oral chlorphenamine — premedication sounds protective, but it does not prevent anaphylaxis and is not recommended.
takeaway: Do not repeat a vaccine that caused anaphylaxis without specialist assessment.

stem:
A 45-year-old man who works as a bus driver is diagnosed with sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis after months of cough and weight loss. His wife, who shares his bedroom, is referred to the TB service for contact screening.

By which route is she most likely to have been exposed?

options.A: Contact with his blood, for example via a shared razor
options.C: Sharing cutlery, crockery and food at mealtimes
options.D: Inhaling droplet nuclei released when he coughs
options.E: Bites from bedbugs or other household insects

correct_answer: D. Inhaling droplet nuclei released when he coughs
why_correct: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is spread by the airborne route: a person with infectious pulmonary disease releases tiny droplet nuclei when coughing, speaking or sneezing, and these remain suspended and are inhaled by others. Prolonged close contact in an enclosed space, such as sharing a bedroom, carries the highest risk, which is why household contacts are screened. Source: Tuberculosis, NICE NG33, 2016 (updated 2019).
why_wrong: A. TB is not a blood-borne infection, so a shared razor is not the route. B. Sexual intercourse is not the transmission route; the risk comes from sharing the same air for long periods. C. Sharing cutlery, crockery and food does not spread pulmonary TB. E. TB has no insect vector.
pearl: Patients with infectious pulmonary TB in hospital should be nursed in a single room, and those with suspected multidrug-resistant disease in a negative-pressure room.
thinking: Smear-positive pulmonary TB ↓ Bacilli released when coughing ↓ Droplet nuclei stay suspended in air ↓ Inhaled by close contacts ↓ Airborne transmission
exam_trap: C, Sharing cutlery, crockery and food — close household sharing is linked to risk, but it is the shared air, not the utensils, that transmits TB.
takeaway: Pulmonary tuberculosis is spread by the airborne route.

stem:
A GP is reviewing preventive care for a 74-year-old man who has just moved into a nursing home. He has type 2 diabetes and heart failure. Last winter, an outbreak of fever, cough and muscle aches in the home led to two hospital admissions.

Which intervention will best reduce his risk of a similar illness this winter?

options.A: Taking a daily vitamin C supplement through the winter months
options.B: A pneumococcal vaccine dose repeated each autumn
options.D: Low-dose amoxicillin taken daily from October to March
options.E: An annual chest X-ray to detect early lung infection

why_correct: The outbreak described is typical of seasonal influenza. Under the UK national immunisation programme, adults aged 65 and over, care-home residents and people with chronic heart disease or diabetes are offered influenza vaccine every autumn, because circulating strains change and protection wanes. Vaccinating residents and staff reduces infections, outbreaks and hospital admissions. Source: Influenza, Green Book chapter 19, UKHSA, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin C has not been shown to prevent influenza. B. Pneumococcal vaccine protects against pneumococcal disease, not influenza, and is not given every year. D. Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent a viral illness and drive antimicrobial resistance. E. Chest radiography has no preventive role.
pearl: The influenza vaccine is reformulated each year to match the strains expected to circulate, which is why it must be repeated annually.
thinking: Care-home resident with comorbidities ↓ Winter outbreak of fever, cough and myalgia ↓ Seasonal influenza ↓ Eligible under the national programme ↓ Annual influenza vaccination
exam_trap: B, Pneumococcal vaccine each autumn — it is also offered to older adults and protects against a winter chest infection, but it does not prevent influenza and is not an annual vaccine.
takeaway: Annual influenza vaccination is the main preventive measure for older and at-risk adults, including care-home residents.

stem:
A newly qualified nurse in a general practice treatment room tells a colleague that she only uses gloves, aprons and careful sharps disposal for patients known to have an infection such as hepatitis or HIV. Her colleague explains how standard infection control precautions should be applied.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: They are needed only for patients with a confirmed or suspected infection
options.B: They apply to hospital wards but not to community clinics
options.C: They make additional transmission-based precautions unnecessary
options.D: They apply to every patient in every setting, at all times
options.E: They are only required during invasive or surgical procedures

correct_answer: D. They apply to every patient in every setting, at all times
why_correct: Standard infection control precautions, such as hand hygiene, appropriate PPE, safe sharps handling and management of blood and body fluids, apply to all patients in all settings. Infection status is often unknown, so every patient is treated as a potential source. The type of PPE is chosen according to the anticipated exposure for each task. Source: National infection prevention and control manual for England, NHS England, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Many people with blood-borne viruses are undiagnosed, so restricting precautions to known cases leaves staff and patients at risk. B. They apply equally in primary care, community and hospital settings. C. Transmission-based precautions, such as airborne or contact isolation, are added on top when a specific infection is suspected. E. They apply to all care activities, including routine examination and specimen handling.
pearl: Transmission-based precautions (contact, droplet or airborne) are always used in addition to, never instead of, standard precautions.
thinking: Nurse uses precautions only for known infection ↓ Infection status is often unknown ↓ Standard precautions are universal ↓ PPE matched to the task ↓ Apply to every patient in every setting
exam_trap: A, Only for known or suspected infection — it seems efficient, but undiagnosed infection is common, which is why precautions are universal.
takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every patient, every time, in every care setting.

stem:
A 34-year-old man attends a drug and alcohol service for a health check. He has injected heroin intermittently for several years and also has tattoos done professionally, plays football in a team, uses a public gym and lives with a partner who shares meals with him.

Which activity puts him at the greatest risk of acquiring hepatitis C?

options.A: Sharing meals and cutlery with his partner at home
options.B: Using the showers and pool at a public gym
options.C: Sharing needles or other injecting equipment
options.D: Close body contact during football matches

correct_answer: C. Sharing needles or other injecting equipment
why_correct: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne virus, and sharing needles, syringes, spoons, filters or water when injecting is the main route of transmission in the UK. Anyone who has ever injected drugs should be offered testing. Sexual and household transmission are uncommon. Source: Hepatitis C in England 2025, UKHSA, 2025.
why_wrong: A. The virus is not transmitted by sharing meals or cutlery. B. Swimming pools and showers are not a route of spread. D. Ordinary sporting contact without blood exposure is not a recognised route. E. Kissing is not a recognised route of transmission.
pearl: Hepatitis C is now curable in most people with 8 to 12 weeks of direct-acting antiviral treatment, so testing people who inject drugs is high value.
thinking: Man who injects drugs ↓ Hepatitis C is blood-borne ↓ Shared injecting equipment carries blood ↓ Casual and household contact do not ↓ Injecting equipment is the main risk
exam_trap: A, Sharing meals and cutlery at home — household contact feels risky, but hepatitis C needs blood exposure and is not spread through food.
takeaway: Sharing injecting equipment is the main route of hepatitis C transmission.

stem:
An 18-year-old university fresher is admitted with meningococcal septicaemia. The health protection team arranges antibiotic prophylaxis for her flatmates and boyfriend but not for the classmates in her lecture group. Her worried mother asks how the infection spreads.

Which route of transmission explains this approach?

options.B: Eating contaminated food prepared in the shared kitchen
options.D: Respiratory droplets and secretions from close contact

correct_answer: D. Respiratory droplets and secretions from close contact
why_correct: Neisseria meningitidis colonises the nasopharynx and spreads through respiratory droplets and direct contact with secretions, for example through intimate kissing or living in the same household. Spread therefore needs prolonged close contact, which is why prophylaxis targets household and intimate contacts rather than casual contacts. Source: Guidance for public health management of meningococcal disease in the UK, UKHSA, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Meningococcus is not spread by insects. B. Contaminated food is not a route of transmission. C. It is not spread by the faecal-oral route. E. Soil is not a reservoir; humans are the only natural host.
pearl: Close contacts of a case of invasive meningococcal disease are offered a single dose of ciprofloxacin as prophylaxis, ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis.
thinking: Invasive meningococcal disease ↓ Organism carried in the nasopharynx ↓ Spread by droplets and secretions ↓ Needs prolonged close contact ↓ Prophylaxis for household and intimate contacts only
exam_trap: B, Contaminated food from a shared kitchen — flatmates share a kitchen, which makes food spread seem plausible, but transmission is via respiratory secretions.
takeaway: Meningococcal infection spreads by respiratory droplets and secretions during close contact.

stem:
A 40-year-old man who recently returned from a stay in a region with an ongoing diphtheria outbreak develops a sore throat, low-grade fever and a grey membrane over the tonsils. Public health staff begin tracing the people he has been near.

By what route is this infection most likely to have spread to him?

options.A: Respiratory droplets from an infected person
options.B: Faecal-oral spread from contaminated drinking water

correct_answer: A. Respiratory droplets from an infected person
why_correct: Respiratory diphtheria, caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae, spreads mainly by respiratory droplets and close contact with secretions from infected people or carriers. The grey adherent pharyngeal membrane after travel to an outbreak area is characteristic. Close contacts need assessment, swabbing, antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination as advised by public health. Source: Public health control and management of diphtheria in England, UKHSA, 2025.
why_wrong: B. Diphtheria is not spread through contaminated water. C. It is not transmitted by mosquitoes. D. Sexual contact is not a typical route. E. Soil is not the source of respiratory diphtheria; cutaneous diphtheria spreads through contact with skin lesions.
pearl: Suspected diphtheria is a notifiable disease and is treated urgently with diphtheria antitoxin plus antibiotics; the toxin can cause myocarditis and neuropathy.
thinking: Recent travel to an outbreak area ↓ Sore throat with grey pharyngeal membrane ↓ Respiratory diphtheria ↓ Spread by droplets and secretions ↓ Close contacts need tracing
exam_trap: E, Contact with soil only — it can be confused with tetanus, another toxin-mediated vaccine-preventable infection, but respiratory diphtheria spreads person to person by droplets.
takeaway: Respiratory diphtheria spreads through respiratory droplets and close contact with infected secretions.

stem:
Two days after a 63-year-old woman was admitted for a planned laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the laboratory reports that one of two sets of blood cultures, taken from separate sites during a brief temperature spike on the night of surgery, has grown coagulase-negative staphylococci. She has no prosthetic heart valve, implanted device or central venous line, her temperature settled within hours, and she is now eating and mobilising. Repeat cultures show no growth.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Occult bacteraemia requiring broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
options.C: Early septic shock requiring fluid resuscitation
options.E: Contamination of the blood culture by skin organisms

correct_answer: E. Contamination of the blood culture by skin organisms
why_correct: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are normal skin flora and a common contaminant introduced when blood cultures are taken. Growth in only one set, in a patient who is clinically well and has negative repeat cultures, makes contamination the most likely explanation. True infection is more likely with multiple positive sets or an indwelling line or implanted prosthetic material. Source: UK Standards for Microbiology Investigations B 37, investigation of blood cultures, UKHSA and Royal College of Pathologists, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Endocarditis typically gives persistently positive cultures in several sets. B. Starting antibiotics for a probable contaminant in a well patient is unnecessary and promotes resistance. C. She is clinically well, so septic shock is not present. D. Nothing suggests meningitis, and a single blood culture does not diagnose it.
pearl: Taking two sets of blood cultures from separate sites with careful skin antisepsis helps distinguish true bacteraemia from contamination.
thinking: Skin organism in one of two sets ↓ Patient now well ↓ Repeat cultures negative ↓ No line, valve or implanted device ↓ Most likely contamination
exam_trap: B, Occult bacteraemia needing broad-spectrum antibiotics — treating every positive culture feels safe, but a single probable contaminant in a well patient does not need antibiotics.
takeaway: A single culture growing a skin organism in a well patient with negative repeats is most likely contamination.
notes: Reviewer fix: Removed new knee prosthesis (CoNS is a true prosthetic-joint pathogen, undermining the contamination key); now laparoscopic cholecystectomy, 'one of two sets from separate sites' instead of one bottle; thinking/why_correct aligned
